Question:
For the consumer, a single discount of \(n\%\) is more advantageous than any of the following discounts:

\((1)\) Two successive \(15\%\) discounts.

\((2)\) Three successive \(10\%\) discounts.

\((3)\) A \(25\%\) discount followed by a \(5\%\) discount.

What is the smallest possible positive integer value of \(n?\)
Solution:
Each successive discount applies to the price remaining after the previous discount, so multiply the retained fractions. As fractions of the same positive original price, the three final prices are
\[
\begin{aligned}
(1)\quad&0.85\cdot0.85=0.7225,\\
(2)\quad&0.90\cdot0.90\cdot0.90=0.729,\\
(3)\quad&0.75\cdot0.95=0.7125.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the effective discounts are \(27.75\%\), \(27.1\%\), and \(28.75\%\), respectively. The third offer gives the lowest price.

A single discount of \(n\%\) leaves the fraction \(1-n/100\) of the original price. To be more advantageous than all three offers, it must leave strictly less than \(0.7125\):
\[
1-\frac{n}{100}<0.7125,
\qquad n>28.75.
\]
The smallest positive integer satisfying this strict inequality is \(29\). It leaves \(71\%\) of the original price, below all three listed prices. The answer is \(29\), choice C.
